title: show ip route
task: Read the routing table and find which next hop a destination will use
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
commands:
show ip route
show ip route 8.8.8.8
show ip route static
show ip route vlan 20
show ip protocols
explain: Routing is **longest-prefix match**, not shortest path. The entry whose mask is most specific wins, regardless of metric.
Codes matter: `C` connected, `L` local, `S` static, `R` RIP, `O` OSPF, `D` EIGRP, `B` BGP, `*` candidate default, `Gateway of last resort` is the fallback when nothing matches.
A connected route appears the moment an interface has an address and is up. If you expect one and it is missing, the interface is down or has no address — that is usually the actual fault.
`show ip protocols` is the one to run when an OSPF adjacency is missing: it shows which networks the process is configured to advertise on which interfaces.
example: Two routes to the same destination: `S 10.0.0.0/8` and `O 10.1.0.0/16`. Traffic for 10.1.2.3 uses the OSPF route, because /16 is longer than /8. Metrics are irrelevant at this step.

errors.means: There is no route matching that destination and no default route. The router has nowhere to send the packet.
errors.fix:
show ip route static
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop>

errors.message: Route is present but traffic still fails
errors.means: Routing is not the problem. The packet is leaving and dying further along, or an ACL is dropping it.
errors.fix:
show ip interface <if> | include line protocol
show access-lists

title: ip route
task: Add a static route, a default route, or a floating backup route
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE global configuration
changes: Yes. Adds an entry to the routing table and to running-config.
risks: A wrong next hop silently blackholes traffic. Over SSH, keep a console session open and use a two-minute revert timer.
explain: The mask is always the **full dotted quad**, never a prefix length. `255.255.255.0`, not `/24`. This is the single most common beginner error.

A **floating static route** has an administrative distance higher than the primary (200 is conventional). It sits in the table but is never used while the primary exists — which is exactly the point, and it does not need `track` on most platforms.
Every static route needs a **reverse path** back, or replies are dropped. If you add a route toward a network and replies do not come back, check that the far end has a route to your source.
Verify with `show ip route` before you leave config mode. A route that is not in the table is not in the router, whatever config says.
example: Primary link to the ISP via 192.168.1.254, backup via a second circuit. The backup uses AD 200 so it only appears if the primary disappears.
verify:
show ip route static
show running-config | include ^ip route

errors.means: You used a prefix length (`ip route 10.20.30.0/24 ...`) or ran it in the wrong mode.
errors.fix: Use: ip route 10.20.30.0 255.255.255.0 <next-hop>, from config mode.

errors.message: Route appears but traffic does not flow
errors.means: Usually a missing return route on the far side, not a problem with this router.
errors.fix: Test both directions: ping from the source, then from the destination back to the source.

title: show spanning-tree
task: Find which port the spanning tree has blocked, and why
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
commands:
show spanning-tree
show spanning-tree vlan 20
show spanning-tree vlan 20 detail
show spanning-tree root
explain: STP blocks redundant paths **on purpose**. A blocked port is not a fault — it is the algorithm working. Chasing it is a classic beginner mistake.
The root bridge is elected by lowest bridge ID, which is priority then MAC. A blocking port forwards normally the moment the primary link fails; that is convergence.
`show spanning-tree vlan X detail` is the one that explains the decision: it prints the root path cost and the priority values that produced the choice.
On a healthy access port you should see `edge` / `portfast` and rapid transition. If it is not edge and the port takes ~30 seconds to forward, portfast was missed.
example: A workstation on Gi0/5 takes 30 seconds to get an IP address after a reboot. That delay is STP listening/learning. `show spanning-tree interface gi0/5` shows the port is not an edge port.

errors.message: A port shows Blocking and you think it is broken
errors.means: It is the redundancy mechanism. Only investigate if the *expected* forwarding port is blocked.
errors.fix: Compare both ends of the link with show spanning-tree vlan <id> detail

title: ip access-list
task: Write an ACL that permits or denies traffic, and place it in the right direction
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE global configuration
changes: Yes. Once applied, traffic may start or stop flowing immediately.
undo: no ip access-list extended NAME   /   no ip access-list standard NAME
risks: **There is an implicit deny any at the end of every ACL.** Apply an ACL that you have not finished writing and you will cut yourself off. Test with a `permit ip any any` first over SSH, then tighten it.
commands:
enable
configure terminal
ip access-list extended BLOCK-GUEST
 permit tcp 10.10.30.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
 permit tcp 10.10.30.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 53
 deny   ip any any log
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/3
 ip access-group BLOCK-GUEST in
end
write memory
show access-lists
explain: **Wildcard masks, not subnet masks.** `0.0.0.255` is "any host in this /24"; `0.0.0.0` is a single host. People swap these constantly. The rule is: 0 means *must match*, 1 means *don't care*.
Order is evaluated top to bottom, first match wins, and evaluation stops there. Putting `deny ip any any` at the top silently overrides everything below it.

Direction matters more than the rule. `in` filters traffic arriving at the interface, `out` filters traffic leaving it. Putting an outbound filter on an interface facing the internet can break your own management session.
ACLs do not log by default. Add `log` when you are diagnosing, and expect it to be noisy on a busy interface — `log-input` is worse.
Always finish an extended ACL with an explicit `deny ip any any log` even though it is implicit, so the intent is visible in the config.
example: Guest VLAN 10.10.30.0/24 should reach the internet and nothing internal. Permit 443 and 53 outbound, then deny everything. Applied `in` on the guest port this enforces both directions of the rule because ACLs are stateless.
verify:
show access-lists
show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/3 | include access list

errors.message: Everything stopped working after applying an ACL
errors.means: The implicit `deny any` caught traffic you did not think about, quite possibly your own management session.
errors.fix:
From a console: no ip access-group NAME in
Then rebuild with explicit permits for what you actually need.

errors.message: The ACL looks right but has no effect
errors.means: Usually applied to the wrong interface or the wrong direction, or the traffic is NATed so the source no longer matches.
errors.fix:
show ip interface <if> | include access list
Confirm the address in the ACL is the address on the wire.

title: show interfaces switchport
task: See the access or trunk mode, the VLAN, and whether the port is actually forwarding
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
commands:
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/5 switchport
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/5 switchport | include Mode|VLAN|edge
show interfaces status
explain: Two lines decide most port faults: **Administrative Mode** is what you configured, **Operational Mode** is what the port negotiated. They can disagree.
`Operational Mode: down` means the port carries nothing at all, whatever the configuration says. Fix that before investigating anything else.
If `Access Mode VLAN` shows `1` when you configured something else, the config did not apply or the VLAN does not exist on this switch.
On trunk ports, `Trunking Native Mode VLAN` and `Trunking VLANs Enabled` tell you what is actually allowed. A VLAN missing from that list is silently dropped, with no error.
example: A client on Gi0/5 gets 169.254.x.x. `show interfaces gi0/5 switchport` shows `Operational Mode: down`. The port never carried a DHCP request, so this is not a DHCP problem.
verify:
show interfaces status
show mac address-table interface GigabitEthernet0/5

errors.message: Access VLAN shows 1 instead of the configured VLAN
errors.means: Either `switchport access vlan` was never applied, or the VLAN does not exist on this switch.
errors.fix:
show vlan brief
Re-apply: switchport access vlan <id>

title: interface / no shutdown
task: Bring a switchport up and give an interface an address
changes: Yes. Brings the interface up and enables routing on it.
risks: On a router interface, `no shutdown` alone starts routing on a link you may not want routed. On a switch, enabling a previously shutdown port exposes whatever is plugged into it.
commands:
enable
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 no shutdown
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 description UPLINK-TO-ROUTER-Gi0/1
 no ip address
 no shutdown
 ip address 10.10.99.2 255.255.255.0
 ip default-gateway 10.10.99.1
end
write memory
show ip interface brief
explain: **Interfaces are administratively shut by default on routers**, and `no shutdown` is required before anything works. Switchports on a Layer-2 switch are usually enabled by default — which is why the habit transfers badly.
`no ip address` on a routed interface removes any address before you set the new one. Without it you can end up with two addresses and confusing routing.
`switchport` on a router interface switches it back to Layer 2 — this is a **Layer-3-to-Layer-2 conversion** and it silently changes every behaviour.
Add a `description` to every port you touch. It is the only thing that will tell you what is plugged in six months from now.
example: A router's WAN interface shows `down, administratively down`. The cable is fine; nobody has run `no shutdown`. This is the single most common first-lab fault.
verify:
show ip interface brief
show interfaces description

errors.message: Interface is up but protocol is down
errors.means: No IP address, or the far end is down. Layer 2 works but Layer 3 has nothing to work with.
errors.fix:
show ip interface brief   → the Protocol column
ip address <addr> <mask>

errors.means: It did — and it just turned a routed port into a switched one. Check `show ip interface` before and after.
errors.fix: no switchport   to return it to Layer 3

title: show mac address-table
task: See which MAC address the switch learned on which port and VLAN
aliases: which port is the pc on
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
commands:
show mac address-table
show mac address-table interface GigabitEthernet0/5
show mac address-table vlan 20
show mac address-table count
show mac address-table dynamic
explain: This is the switch's forwarding table and it is the most useful command in Layer-2 troubleshooting. It is MAC address, port, VLAN.
An entry **flapping between two ports** means a duplicate MAC address somewhere — two devices claiming the same address, or a loop.
No entry for a device that is switched on means its frames are not arriving: check the port, the VLAN and whether anything is bridging.
The table ages out after ~5 minutes of silence, so it reflects *recent* traffic, not the whole network. An idle device legitimately has no entry.
example: PC1 and PC2 are in VLAN 20 on the same switch but cannot reach each other. `show mac address-table vlan 20` shows PC1's MAC but not PC2's. PC2's frames are not arriving — look at its port, not at IP settings.

errors.message: A MAC keeps moving between two ports
errors.means: Duplicate MAC, or a Layer-2 loop. Check for a switch plugged into itself, or an unmanaged switch bridging two segments.
errors.fix:
show spanning-tree   (a loop shows as repeated TCN/ topology changes)
Then isolate the offending segment

title: copy running-config startup-config
task: Save the running configuration so it survives a reboot
where: Cisco IOS / IOS XE privileged EXEC
undo: No undo. That is the point — once saved, the change is permanent across reboots.
risks: Saving a configuration you have not verified turns a temporary lab mistake into a permanent one. In production, change control means an unreviewed save is a process failure even when the config is correct.
commands:
enable
show running-config
copy running-config startup-config
show startup-config | include hostname
write memory
explain: `running-config` is RAM and is lost on reboot. `startup-config` is NVRAM and survives. **Nothing is saved until you copy.**
`write memory` is a long-standing alias for the same command. Both work; `write memory` is what most older documentation shows.
Read `show running-config` **before** copying. This one habit prevents most accidental permanent changes.
In Packet Tracer and in every lab, skipping the save is why a configuration mysteriously disappears between sessions.
example: You configure a VLAN, ping successfully, then reboot during a break. After the reboot the VLAN is gone. You never saved.
verify:
show running-config | include ^hostname
show startup-config | include ^hostname

errors.means: The copy command is asking for confirmation. Press Enter to accept the default.
